fact.fact: Tanzania has an estimated 17,200 lions, the largest population in the world.

body: Tanzania's National Wildlife Census 2024/2025 was the first survey to cover every ecological system in the country. It was led by the Tanzania Wildlife Research Institute, known as Tawiri, and released in Arusha a decade after the previous count.

The headline finding was a steep fall in elephants, from more than 134,000 in 2005 to 66,714. That placed Tanzania third in Africa for elephants, behind Botswana at about 130,000 and Zimbabwe at around 100,000.

The same census counted about 328,000 buffalo, the highest number in Africa, and an estimated 17,200 lions, also the largest population on the continent. Tanzania also holds around 302 black rhinos, ranking fifth in Africa.

Tawiri's director general, Eblate Mjingo, described mixed fortunes: several species are recovering while elephants remain under pressure. Conservation officials pointed to poaching in the early and mid-2000s, and now to expanding settlements, farming and infrastructure that fragment habitats and cut migration corridors.
deepDive.whyItMatters: The census shows that a country can lose more than half its elephants in two decades and still hold the world's largest populations of lions and buffalo. That breadth is what allows Tanzania's nature-based tourism to keep growing, with receipts rising from about US$3.9 billion to around US$4.4 billion, even as its flagship species declines.

fact.fact: Ubuntu operating system was founded in 2004 by South African entrepreneur Mark Shuttleworth.

body: In October 2004, a new computer operating system called Ubuntu was released. Its development was led by Mark Shuttleworth, a South African entrepreneur who owns the UK-based company Canonical Ltd.

The name was not chosen at random. Ubuntu is a Bantu philosophy that emphasises the interconnectedness of people, often summed up as "I am because we are". By naming the software after this concept, Shuttleworth connected a global technology project to a long-standing African idea about community and shared humanity.

The operating system went on to become widely used around the world, and the name introduced many outside Africa to the word ubuntu. The philosophy itself has a much deeper history, appearing in South African written sources as early as the mid-19th century and later shaping political transitions in Zimbabwe and South Africa.
deepDive.whyItMatters: The name Ubuntu carried a specific African philosophy into living rooms and offices far beyond the continent. Every time someone installs or updates the software, they are repeating a word that, in several Bantu languages, means humanity.

fact.fact: Ubuntu is an Nguni Bantu term meaning "humanity", part of a concept translated as "I am because we are".

body: The word ubuntu comes from the Nguni Bantu languages of southern Africa. It means "humanity", but it carries more than a dictionary definition. The concept behind it is often rendered in English as "I am because we are", or "I am because you are".

In Zulu the idea appears in the phrase umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu, which points to "humanity towards others". In Xhosa the same kind of term is used, often with a more philosophical weight: a belief in a universal bond of sharing that connects all humanity.

Across different ethnic groups the details of these values and practices vary. What they share is a single direction: an authentic human being is understood as part of a larger relational, communal, societal, environmental and spiritual world.

That framing sits inside a wider pattern in traditional African religions, where the community, the family and the environment all play a role in a person's life. Virtue itself is often tied to carrying out communal obligations, such as respecting parents and elders, raising children well, offering hospitality, and being honest, trustworthy and courageous.
deepDive.whyItMatters: Ubuntu is often quoted as a proverb, but it belongs to a set of values that treat personhood as something built through relationships rather than held alone. In the wider context of traditional African religions, that same emphasis shows up in how virtue is defined: not as private belief, but as carrying out obligations to family, elders and community.
